look_here_first: FIND A HORIZONTAL RUNNER first: slender tough ABOVEGROUND STOLONS root and branch at nodes, and mature mats usually ALSO have BELOWGROUND RHIZOMES with pale papery/scaly nodes. Pull a leaf blade gently back at its collar: look for a very SHORT ligule made of a FRINGE OF WHITE HAIRS (not a clear triangular membrane) and tufts of longer hairs on the collar shoulders. If flowering, look for 3–7 (often 4–6) THIN FINGER-LIKE SEEDHEAD BRANCHES coming from nearly ONE POINT at the stem tip, each bearing tiny spikelets on ONE SIDE in two rows. Don't ID only from a 'star seedhead': crabgrass and goosegrass imitate it.

taxonomic_note: Cynodon dactylon (L.) Pers. is an accepted perennial Poaceae species, and Kew POWO lists Texas as INTRODUCED, not native. Common lawn bermudagrass and C. dactylon × C. transvaalensis hybrids (often fine, vigorous, vegetatively propagated turf lines) can be difficult to assign exactly from a mowed sterile patch. 'Bermuda' is a common name, not evidence of a Bermudian native origin. Texas nonnative label is clear; BONAP county-by-county audit not needed to identify this as introduced.

project_inclusion.native_range_decision: Kew POWO native Old World to Australia; Texas introduced.
project_inclusion.restoration_policy: Mark as introduced aggressive turf/invader in native beds and field restoration; horticultural turf use is a different management setting.

best_field_traits: Warm-season perennial forming tightly interlocking mats of rooting slender runners (STOLONS) and scaly branching underground RHIZOMES.
Flowering stems typically 5–40 cm high. Narrow usually 1–4 mm wide leaf blades are short, pointed and often folded/rolled in bud; leaf color, width and height vary by mowing and turf cultivar.
Short LIGULE about 0.5 mm, consisting largely of a row/fringe of fine hairs at blade-sheath junction; collar usually bears conspicuous long hairs or tufts toward shoulders. No auricles.
Flowering head: usually 4–6 fingerlike unilateral spikes (range roughly 2–9) radiate together in one terminal whorl, each ~2–6 cm long.
Each seedhead branch bears TWO tight rows of one-sided small spikelets, usually ~2–3.2 mm long, attached to a narrow rachis, not showy florets.

Stolons are on the surface and often reddish or straw-green, with nodes that may sprout roots and shoots; underground runners have scaly/papery nodes. Both underground and aboveground spread may survive mowing.
Compare crabgrass and goosegrass with same silhouette by ligule type, origin/spacing of finger-like spikes and perennial subterranean rhizomes.
morphology_keys.growth_habit: Aggressively spreading, mat-forming perennial warm-season grass; spreads via wiry horizontal aboveground stolons and belowground rhizomes, plus viable seeds in many common types.
morphology_keys.stolon: Long prostrate running stem visible on soil surface, rooting at nodes where adequate moisture contacts ground, with short upright leafy shoots at nodes; usually fine, wiry and resilient under frequent mowing.
morphology_keys.rhizome: Stiffer scaly underground runner with pointed/budding nodes, often within upper soil profile; can penetrate further in favorable conditions. Not simply roots: rhizomes have nodes/buds and can sprout new stems.
morphology_keys.culm: Erect/ascending flowering stems usually 5–40(-50) cm, nodes apparent, stems not woody; growing culms and turf mats variable by management.
morphology_keys.leaf_blade: Linear narrow green to gray-green blades, generally ~1–6 cm long (can be to 16) and 1–4 mm wide; acutely tipped, flat or folded; smooth to occasionally sparsely hairy upper surface. Leaf width is not a species identifier across turf hybrids.
morphology_keys.leaf_sheath: Open sheath encircling lower culm; smooth or sparse hairs; faint papery sleeves at runner nodes. Long collar hairs frequent.
morphology_keys.collar: Both sides of short grass collar commonly have long white hairs. Hairs along the ligule are different from scattered leaf blade hairs; use a 10× hand lens to distinguish.
morphology_keys.ligule: Very short FRINGE of fine whitish hairs (~0.5 mm). Not a tall solid membranous ligule. Auricles absent.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Terminal digitate or subdigitate panicle with usually 4–6 thin branches (extremes 2–9), mostly radiating from nearly one point; branches 2–6 cm, narrow and one-sided.
morphology_keys.spikelet: 1-flowered principal spikelets 2–3.2 mm, compressed and arranged in 2 rows along one side of each slender finger branch; glumes shorter than lemmas, awns usually absent.
morphology_keys.seed: Grain (caryopsis) within a small fertile spikelet; some selected hybrid turf types are sterile and do not set viable seed.
morphology_keys.roots: Fibrous and from rooting nodes; do not mistake old fibrous roots for rhizomes: only rhizomes have joints/scales/buds.
morphology_keys.phenology: Warm-season active growth and flowering during hotter brighter months; foliage frequently browns after frost, while perennial stolon/rhizome systems can survive.
morphology_keys.habitat: High-sun turf, trails and road edges, vacant lots, disturbed soils, irrigated sites, park transitions, native meadow edges and beds invaded from adjacent mowed turf.
morphology_keys.variation: Highly variable vegetative phenotype under mowing, cultivar selection and hybridization with C. transvaalensis. Fertile flower-head and belowground runner morphology are stronger than leaf color alone.

comparisons.look_here_first: Star/finger seedheads are a TRAP: make three checks. (1) Are fingers inserted at ONE whorl or staggered along top of stem? (2) Do aboveground stolons AND underground scaly rhizomes connect this mat? (3) Is ligule a short HAIR FRINGE or a membranous flap? Retain Poaceae sp. or Cynodon sp. for sterile cultivar/hybrid uncertainties.

crew_key: 1. Show whether the grass forms slender, rooting surface runners. No? Inspect goosegrass/crabgrass/dallisgrass instead.
2. Check under the turf edge for SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOMES WITH NODES as well as surface stolons. Both → bermudagrass strongly favored.
3. Open a blade at the leaf sheath: tiny hairy-fringed ligule and tufts along collar. Clear membrane → consider Digitaria/Eleusine/Paspalum.
4. When flowering, count thin DIGITATE fingers originating almost together, typically 3–7; check spikelets only on ONE SIDE of each finger.
5. If the finger spikes arise at slightly different heights → Digitaria. If thick fingers over a flattened white crown and only fibrous roots → Eleusine. If several whorls occur up stalk → Chloris.
6. For mowed, sterile, fine turf cultivars, avoid subspecies/hybrid certainty and use Cynodon sp. / bermudagrass turf complex.
comparisons.warning: Fertilization, mowing, drought, shade and breeding can obscure classic leaf/seedhead characters. Buffalograss and Chloris are important native lookalikes; do not call every low stolon-forming native-looking grass bermuda without examining both runners and reproductive structures.

family_genus_teaching.family: Poaceae. Look for nodes, open sheath, COLLAR, LIGULE, alternate two-ranked grass blades and spikelets; the visible finger head is not a single flower but repeated tiny florets inside spikelets.
family_genus_teaching.genus: Cynodon has perennial turf/sprawling habit; small slender unilateral spikelike racemes radiate from one terminal point. Collar and rhizomes help distinguish from Digitaria and Eleusine.
family_genus_teaching.species: C. dactylon: vigorous aboveground rooting stolons plus underground scaly rhizomes, usually several delicate finger spikes, short hairs for ligule, collar tufts. Texas is INTRODUCED on Kew POWO.
family_genus_teaching.crew_prompt: Lift a patch edge, trace an aboveground stolon with roots at its joints, dig just enough to spot a scaly rhizome, then show me the collar hairs and where the finger spikes originate. Can you name each part?

ecological_notes.texas_native_status: Introduced/non-native to Texas per Kew POWO. No regional native-zone uncertainty warrants planting it as a native; maintain separate from confirmed native grass selections.
ecological_notes.restoration_impact: Rapid vegetative spread, dense mat and persistence can suppress establishment of native seedlings and displace the intended lower grass/forb layer in sunny disturbed restoration sites. It can reinvade from adjacent irrigated turf or path edges.
ecological_notes.ecosystem_caveat: Can provide soil cover/erosion protection and forage in managed turf or livestock systems but those functions do not establish it as equivalent to diverse native grass/forb habitat.
ecological_notes.management_priority: Map advancing stolon edges, mark patch boundaries, identify source lawn edges, avoid dragging live rhizomes to new native beds. Treat turf and native-conservation zones differently; prioritize monitoring after disturbance.
ecological_notes.nonchemical_control: Manual removal must include viable stolons AND rhizomes; repeated careful digging/sifting on small patches, black opaque coverings or repeated drying under hot weather can help. Do not till wet infestations into fragments that root. Large existing infestations may require extended follow-up and integrated methods, no one-pass cure.
ecological_notes.crew_safety: When extracting during wet soil conditions, bag stems/nodes; avoid moving cuttings into compost or soil unless guaranteed dead. Document resprouts, mowing timing and persistence.
ecological_notes.native_alternatives: Site-dependent short native-grass candidates include Bouteloua dactyloides (buffalograss) and Bouteloua gracilis (blue grama); these are not visually or structurally interchangeable with bermudagrass, and plant palette should follow local BONAP ranges, site moisture and full species diversity.
ecological_notes.cultivated_hybrid_caution: C. dactylon × C. transvaalensis turf hybrids and improved cultivars are still nonnative turfgrass; exact hybrid attribution cannot be proved by leaf shape alone.
ecological_notes.lep_bee_note: Do not invent larval host counts or specialist bee associations. Link exact verified evidence if dashboard provides it.
